blocks.text: A double-glazed window loses heat through a still layer of air that is not quite still: if the cavity is wide, a slow circulation develops that carries more heat across the gap than conduction alone. Predicting that extra heat is what natural convection correlations are for.

blocks.markdown: The dimensionless result of natural convection analysis is $\overline{Nu}=f(Ra,Pr)$. No theory gives a closed form for most geometries, so correlations fitted to experiments are used. For each correlation you must state the geometry, the characteristic length, the property temperature (the film temperature $T_f$) and the validity range in $Ra$.

blocks.title: Natural convection correlation
blocks.text: $\overline{Nu}_L=\bar hL/k$ is the average Nusselt number based on the characteristic length $L$ (vertical height for plates and walls; the plate separation for an enclosure). All fluid properties are evaluated at $T_f=(T_s+T_\infty)/2$ and $\beta=1/T_f$ for a gas.

blocks.caption: Isothermal vertical plate or wall, laminar and turbulent ranges (McAdams form), properties at the film temperature

blocks.title: Heat loss from a heated vertical panel
blocks.prompt: A vertical panel 0.6 m high and 1.5 m wide is held at 50 $^\circ$C in still air at 20 $^\circ$C. Use air properties at the film temperature (typical): $\nu=1.6\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s, $\alpha=2.25\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s, $k=0.026$ W/m K. Estimate the convection coefficient and the heat loss from one face.

steps.text: This lies between $10^4$ and $10^9$ (laminar), so use $\overline{Nu}_L=0.59\,Ra_L^{1/4}$: $\overline{Nu}_L=0.59\times154.72=91.28$.

blocks.answer: $Ra_L\approx5.73e+08$, $\bar h\approx4.0$ W/m$^2$K and $q\approx107$ W per face. A value of a few W/m$^2$K is typical for air in natural convection.

blocks.markdown: A fluid layer between two horizontal plates behaves differently according to which plate is hot. If the upper plate is hotter, the light fluid sits above the heavy fluid, so the layer is stable and heat moves by conduction alone ($Nu=1$). If the lower plate is hotter, the layer is unstable. Motion starts only when $Ra_L$ exceeds about 1708; below that, conduction is the only mechanism ($Nu=1$).

blocks.caption: Horizontal enclosure heated from below, L the gap between the plates, Ra_L built on the temperature difference across the gap

blocks.title: Horizontal air layer heated from below
blocks.prompt: Two large horizontal plates are 60 mm apart with air between them. The lower plate is at 60 $^\circ$C and the upper plate at 20 $^\circ$C. Use air properties at the mean temperature (typical): $\nu=1.7\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s, $\alpha=2.4\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s, $k=0.027$ W/m K, $Pr=0.71$. Find the heat flux across the layer and compare with pure conduction.

steps.text: Mean temperature $=313.15$ K, $\beta=1/313.15$ K$^{-1}$. The characteristic length is the gap $L=0.060$ m. $Ra_L=9.81\times(1/313.15)\times40\times0.06^3/(1.7\times10^{-5}\times2.4\times10^{-5})=6.634e+05$.
The warm fluid is below, so the layer is unstable and cellular motion occurs once $Ra_L>1708$. For $3\times10^5<Ra_L<7\times10^9$ use $\overline{Nu}_L=0.069\,Ra_L^{1/3}Pr^{0.074}$.
Heat flux $q''=\bar h(T_h-T_c)=2.64\times40=105.6$ W/m$^2$. Pure conduction would give $k\Delta T/L=18.0$ W/m$^2$, so convection raises the transfer by a factor $Nu=5.87$.

blocks.answer: $Ra_L\approx6.63e+05$, $\overline{Nu}_L\approx5.9$ and $q''\approx106$ W/m$^2$, about 5.9 times the conduction-only value of 18 W/m$^2$.

blocks.caption: Natural convection correlations used in this unit

blocks.markdown: To judge whether natural convection matters, compare coefficients. Typical orders of magnitude for gases are about 2 to 25 W/m$^2$K in natural convection and 25 to 250 W/m$^2$K in forced convection. In many problems the forced $h$ is an order of magnitude larger and natural convection can be ignored; for a hot component in still air it is the only convection mechanism.

items: Identify the geometry and the characteristic length $L$ (height or gap).
Evaluate properties at $T_f$ and compute $\beta=1/T_f$ for a gas.
Compute $Ra_L$ and select the correlation by checking its range.
Compute $\bar h=\overline{Nu}_Lk/L$ and then $q=\bar hA\Delta T$.
Compare with the forced convection coefficient if flow is present.

blocks.title: Heated from below versus above
blocks.text: A horizontal layer cooled from below (hot plate on top) is stable and has $Nu=1$, so using the enclosure correlation would overestimate the heat transfer. Also check the lower $Ra$ limit: below 1708 for a layer heated from below there is no convection, and the correlation is not valid.

blocks.title: Scaling
blocks.text: In the laminar vertical range, $\bar h\propto\Delta T^{1/4}L^{-1/4}$ so heat loss $\propto\Delta T^{5/4}$. In the turbulent range ($Nu\propto Ra^{1/3}$) $\bar h$ does not depend on the height $L$, since $L^3$ cancels one $1/L$.

points: Horizontal layer heated from below: $\overline{Nu}_L=0.069Ra_L^{1/3}Pr^{0.074}$ for $3\times10^5<Ra_L<7\times10^9$; conduction only if $Ra_L<1708$ or if heated from above.
Evaluate properties at the film temperature and $\beta=1/T_f$ for gases; $\bar h=\overline{Nu}k/L$.
Natural convection in air gives $h\approx2$ to $25$ W/m$^2$K; forced convection is usually much greater.

questions.stem: The correlation $\overline{Nu}_L=0.59\,Ra_L^{1/4}$ for an isothermal vertical plate applies for

options.text: any $Ra_L$, as the exponent 1/4 is exact

distractorRationale.b: The turbulent range uses the coefficient 0.10 and the exponent 1/3.
distractorRationale.c: Below the threshold of 1708 applies to the horizontal enclosure heated from below, not to vertical plates.
distractorRationale.d: The correlation is empirical and valid only inside its range.

questions.explanation: The 1/4 power law reflects a laminar layer whose thickness grows steadily with height. Above $Ra_L=10^9$ the layer is turbulent and the 1/3 power law applies.

questions.stem: Typical average heat transfer coefficients for air are about

options.text: 25 to 250 W/m$^2$K for natural convection and 2 to 25 W/m$^2$K for forced convection
2 to 25 W/m$^2$K for natural convection and 25 to 250 W/m$^2$K for forced convection
500 to 10000 W/m$^2$K for natural convection of air
Natural and forced convection are identical for air

questions.correctOptionText: 2 to 25 W/m$^2$K for natural convection and 25 to 250 W/m$^2$K for forced convection

distractorRationale.a: The ranges are reversed; forced flow has the larger coefficient.
distractorRationale.c: These magnitudes are typical of boiling or condensation.
distractorRationale.d: Forced flow thins the boundary layer and gives larger $h$.

questions.explanation: Natural convection in air gives low coefficients because buoyancy-driven velocities are small, while a fan can raise $h$ by an order of magnitude. These ranges are typical and not exact.

questions.stem: A vertical wall 0.8 m high is at 45 $^\circ$C in air at 20 $^\circ$C. Take the film temperature as 305.65 K, with $\nu=1.6\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s, $\alpha=2.25\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s, $k=0.026$ W/m K. Use $\overline{Nu}_L=0.59Ra_L^{1/4}$ for $Ra_L<10^9$ and $0.10Ra_L^{1/3}$ for $Ra_L>10^9$. Find the average heat transfer coefficient in W/m$^2$K.
questions.explanation: $Ra_L=9.81\times(1/305.65)\times25\times0.8^3/(1.6\times10^{-5}\times2.25\times10^{-5})=1.141e+09$, which exceeds $10^9$, so the turbulent form applies. $\overline{Nu}_L=0.10\times1045.0=104.50$ and $\bar h=104.50\times0.026/0.8=3.40$ W/m$^2$K.

questions.stem: The lower plate of a solar collector is at 80 $^\circ$C and the glass cover above it at 30 $^\circ$C, 60 mm apart, with a horizontal air layer between them (mean temperature 328.15 K; $\nu=1.85\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s, $\alpha=2.6\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s, $k=0.028$ W/m K, $Pr=0.71$). Use $\overline{Nu}_L=0.069Ra_L^{1/3}Pr^{0.074}$. Find the heat flux across the gap in W/m$^2$.

A vertical plate 0.30 m tall at 40 $^\circ$C stands in air at 20 $^\circ$C ($T_f=303.15$ K, $\nu=1.6\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s, $\alpha=2.25\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s, $k=0.026$ W/m K, $Pr=0.71$). Compare natural convection ($\overline{Nu}_L=0.59Ra_L^{1/4}$) with a forced laminar flow of 2.0 m/s along the plate ($\overline{Nu}_L=0.664Re_L^{1/2}Pr^{1/3}$). Find the ratio of the forced to the natural convection coefficient (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: Natural: $Ra_L=4.854e+07$, $\overline{Nu}_L=0.59Ra_L^{1/4}=49.25$ and $\bar h_n=4.27$ W/m$^2$K. Forced: $Re_L=2\times0.3/(1.6\times10^{-5})=37500$, $\overline{Nu}_L=0.664\times193.6\times0.8921=114.7$ and $\bar h_f=9.94$ W/m$^2$K. Ratio $=2.33$, so natural convection would be neglected only if the forced coefficient is much larger.

questions.stem: A horizontal air layer is bounded by a hot upper plate and a cooler lower plate. Heat transfer across the layer is by

options.text: conduction only, since the layer is stably stratified
radiation only, since conduction in gases is zero

questions.correctOptionText: conduction only, since the layer is stably stratified

distractorRationale.b: Cellular motion occurs only when the warm fluid is below the cold fluid.
distractorRationale.c: This enclosure correlation is for layers heated from below.
distractorRationale.d: Gases conduct heat, and radiation is a separate mechanism.

questions.explanation: With the lighter, warmer fluid already on top there is no buoyancy-driven overturning, so heat moves by conduction ($Nu=1$, plus radiation). Instability and cellular convection need the hot surface below.

questions.stem: Heat transfer across a horizontal air layer heated from below is in the range where $\overline{Nu}_L=0.069Ra_L^{1/3}Pr^{0.074}$. If the gap $L$ is doubled with the same plate temperatures and fluid, the average coefficient $\bar h$

options.text: doubles, since the gap is larger
increases by a factor of 8, since $Ra\propto L^3$
is unchanged, because $L^3$ in $Ra$ cancels the $1/L$ in $\bar h=Nu\,k/L$

questions.correctOptionText: is unchanged, because $L^3$ in $Ra$ cancels the $1/L$ in $\bar h=Nu\,k/L$

distractorRationale.a: $Nu\propto L$ in this range, so $h=Nu\,k/L$ does not depend on $L$.
distractorRationale.b: $Nu$ also increases with $L$ (as $L$ to the first power).
distractorRationale.c: $Nu$ varies as $Ra^{1/3}$, so the $L^3$ gives $Nu\propto L$, not $L^3$.

questions.explanation: $Nu\propto Ra^{1/3}\propto L$, so $\bar h=Nu\,k/L$ is independent of the gap in this range. This is why widening a cavity beyond a point does not reduce its heat transfer coefficient.

questions.stem: A student must find the natural convection heat loss from a hot vertical plate and a hot horizontal air gap. Describe how you would choose the correlation for each, listing what must be checked before using it.
markingGuide: Identify geometry and characteristic length (height for the plate, gap for the layer).
Evaluate properties at the film (mean) temperature and use $\beta=1/T$ for a gas.
Compute $Ra_L$ and check the validity range (for the plate $10^4<Ra<10^9$ laminar or $10^9<Ra<10^{13}$ turbulent; for the layer $3\times10^5<Ra<7\times10^9$).
For the layer check which plate is hotter: heated from above gives $Nu=1$, and $Ra<1708$ gives conduction only.
Convert to $\bar h$ and heat transfer.
questions.explanation: The point is that no single formula applies: both geometry and range must be checked. The layer correlation is only for unstable heating from below.

questions.stem: For a heated vertical plate in the laminar range show that the heat loss varies as $\Delta T^{5/4}$, and say why in the turbulent range the coefficient is independent of plate height.
markingGuide: Laminar: $\overline{Nu}_L=0.59Ra_L^{1/4}$ with $Ra_L\propto\Delta TL^3$, so $\bar h=\overline{Nu}k/L\propto\Delta T^{1/4}L^{-1/4}$.
Heat loss $q=\bar hA\Delta T\propto\Delta T^{1/4}\times\Delta T=\Delta T^{5/4}$.
Turbulent: $\overline{Nu}_L\propto Ra_L^{1/3}\propto\Delta T^{1/3}L$, so $\bar h=\overline{Nu}k/L\propto\Delta T^{1/3}$.
The $L$ cancels because turbulent mixing makes the boundary layer thickness roughly independent of height, so $h$ is the same at any height.
questions.explanation: The exponent follows from the power-law dependence on $Ra$ and the fact that the heat loss includes a further factor of $\Delta T$. Independence of $L$ in the turbulent regime is a characteristic result of the 1/3 power law.

questions.stem: A glass window 1.5 m tall and 1.0 m wide has an inner surface at 5 $^\circ$C facing a room at 20 $^\circ$C ($T_f=285.65$ K, $\nu=1.5\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s, $\alpha=2.1\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s, $k=0.025$ W/m K). Use $0.59Ra_L^{1/4}$ for $Ra_L<10^9$ and $0.10Ra_L^{1/3}$ above $10^9$. Find the convective heat gain to the window surface in W (ignore radiation).
questions.explanation: $Ra_L=9.81\times(1/285.65)\times15\times1.5^3/(1.5\times10^{-5}\times2.1\times10^{-5})=5.519e+09$, which is above $10^9$, so $\overline{Nu}_L=0.10Ra_L^{1/3}=176.7$. Then $\bar h=176.7\times0.025/1.5=2.95$ W/m$^2$K and $q=\bar hA\Delta T=2.95\times1.5\times15=66.3$ W.
